title: Salman Khan Just Went to War Over a Film He Didn't Make. The Bracelet Gave It Away.
excerpt: Delhi High Court issues notices after the superstar's legal team argues Kala Hiran: Battle for Legacy uses his likeness, his signature turquoise bracelet, and his still-pending poaching case for profit. The next hearing is June 19.
body:
There is exactly one bracelet in Bollywood that doesn't need a name attached to it. Turquoise, chunky, never off his wrist — it belongs to **Salman Khan** the way the fedora belonged to Sinatra. So when a poster for an obscure indie film called *Kala Hiran: Battle for Legacy* surfaced on May 29 featuring a man styled to look unmistakably like the superstar — bracelet and all — the internet noticed. And then Salman's lawyers got involved.

The Delhi High Court on Friday issued notices to the makers of *Kala Hiran* after Khan filed a plea seeking an immediate ban on the film's production, promotion, and release. Justice **Neena Bansal Krishna** directed notices to producer **Amit Jani**, production house **Jani FireFox Films**, director **Bharat Shrinate**, and casting director **Akshay Pandey**, scheduling the next hearing for June 19.

## The Case: Personality Rights and a Lookalike



> **"## The Case: Personality Rights and a Lookalike

According to the petition, the film's lead character — named *Ayan Khan*, played by actor **Kashif Iqbal Khan** — is explicitly modelled after Salman."**


According to the petition, the film's lead character — named *Ayan Khan*, played by actor **Kashif Iqbal Khan** — is explicitly modelled after Salman. The styling, the posture, the bracelet, the firearm in the poster. Khan's advocate **Nizam Pasha** told the court that the resemblance is no coincidence: the film is inspired by the 1998 blackbuck poaching case in Jodhpur, a matter that remains sub judice before the Rajasthan High Court and the Supreme Court.

> "The promotional materials feature the character holding a firearm, which creates a highly misleading narrative given that the actor was officially acquitted in the related Arms Act proceedings in January 2017." — Court filing

The petition also references media interviews and a press conference by producer Amit Jani, in which the film was described as being inspired by the blackbuck controversy and the long-running tension involving gangster **Lawrence Bishnoi**. For Salman's team, this is the smoking gun: the film isn't just *about* a poaching case. It's about *his* poaching case, dressed up in a thin fictional wrapper.

## A Court Order Already Existed

This isn't Salman's first move to protect his image. On December 11, 2025, the Delhi High Court had already passed an interim order safeguarding the actor's personality rights — a broad legal shield that prevents the unauthorized commercial exploitation of a public figure's identity, likeness, and associated attributes.

Khan's legal team sent a cease-and-desist notice to the filmmakers on April 24, 2026, demanding they halt all work. According to the petition, the warning was ignored. The trailer dropped on Friday — ahead of its previously announced June 20 date — even as the legal proceedings were underway. That accelerated timeline, Pasha argued, suggests the makers were trying to get ahead of the court.

## Death Threats and Defiance

The story took a darker turn when producer Amit Jani alleged that he received death threats following the filing of Khan's lawsuit. No further details have been made public, but the claim adds a menacing layer to what is already Bollywood's most charged legal confrontation of the year.

For the diaspora watching from abroad, the case is a fascinating collision of celebrity law, creative freedom, and India's still-evolving personality rights jurisprudence. The question at its centre isn't just whether *Kala Hiran* borrows Salman's image — it's whether anyone can dramatise a living star's most infamous chapter without their consent.

## What Happens Next

The Delhi High Court will hear the matter again on **June 19**. Until then, the trailer is out, the poster is everywhere, and the bracelet that started it all remains firmly on Salman Khan's wrist — where, if his lawyers have anything to say about it, it will stay exclusively his.
